Turn row-level data into single summary values. Learn how COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX provide fast answers for reporting and analysis.

screens.title: What are Group (Aggregate) Functions?
screens.narratorSegment: Group functions, also called aggregate functions, compute a single summary value from a set of rows. They do not return one result per row; instead they examine a selection of rows and produce one number or value that describes that set. For example, if you ask for the total salary across all employees, you are taking many salary values and producing one total. A concrete example: an employees table with multiple salary entries will yield one SUM value when you sum the salary column. This is different from non-aggregate queries that list each employee. A common misconception is to expect aggregates to preserve row-level detail — they do not. If you need both summaries and details, you must combine aggregates with grouping clauses, but that is outside this screen's core definition. Why it matters: aggregates let you replace tedious manual calculations with a single S Q L expression, which scales to millions of rows. Example scenario: HR wants total payroll for a quarter; a SUM on salary returns that single payroll number instantly. Consider: when you see one aggregated number, ask which rows were included and whether NULL values or DISTINCT uniqueness affected the result. How will you check which rows an aggregate summarized?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › What are Group Functions?
Definition

Group functions produce a single summary value

They operate on sets of rows to return a count, total, average, minimum, or maximum. Aggregates are essential for reporting and analysis.

• Aggregate query returns one value for the chosen set, not one per row.
• Aggregates ignore NULLs in the column being aggregated unless you replace them.
• Use NVL or COALESCE to substitute values when you must include NULLs in calculations.
Concrete Example
Imagine an employees table with five rows of salary values. A SUM on salary returns one total pay number. If a salary is NULL, SUM ignores that row. If HR expects NULL to mean zero, you must replace NULLs first.
-- Visual starter queries (for reference)
-- Total number of employees
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;

-- Total salary
SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees;

-- Average salary (ignores NULLs)
SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees;
Key Takeaway

Group functions summarize rows into one value. Always confirm which rows were included and whether NULLs or DISTINCT changed the result.

screens.title: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)
screens.narratorSegment: COUNT is frequently misused because people assume every COUNT returns the same thing. There are two common forms to know: counting all rows and counting non‑null values in a column. COUNT star counts every row in the chosen set, including rows that have nulls in other columns. By contrast, COUNT with a column name counts only rows where that column is not null. A concrete example: an employees table with five rows, one salary set to null. COUNT star returns five, while counting salary returns four. That difference matters when you report headcount versus the number of employees with salary recorded. A typical misconception is thinking COUNT column equals total rows; this leads to underreporting when nulls exist. When you need the total rows regardless of nulls, use the all-rows form. When you need how many valid entries a column contains, use the column form. Practice: run both forms and compare results to confirm which rows were ignored. Which count aligns with your reporting goal? COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) means count star returns all rows; count(column) returns only non-null column entries. pick the form that matches your question.. In practical terms, how counting all rows differs from counting non-null column values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)
Scenario

Counting rows or non-null values?

Compare the two forms to choose the correct count for your report: headcount or number of recorded values.

• COUNT star includes every row, so it measures the total number of records.
• COUNT with a column name measures how many rows have a non-null entry in that column.
• Use COUNT(column) when you want the number of valid entries in a field; use COUNT star for total rows.
Concrete Example
Employees sample: five rows, one salary NULL. COUNT star gives five. COUNT salary gives four. When reporting headcount, prefer the all-rows count.
Visual Comparison
COUNT(*)
Counts all rows. Use for total record counts or headcount metrics.
Example result: 5
COUNT(salary)
Counts only non-null salary entries. Use for valid value counts.
Example result: 4
Common Mistake

Assuming COUNT(column) counts rows. Always check for NULLs if you expected the total number of rows.

screens.title: SUM and AVG with NULLs and NVL
screens.narratorSegment: SUM and AVG are straightforward in intent but subtle in behavior when nulls are present. SUM totals all non-null numeric values. AVG computes the arithmetic mean of non-null values only, dividing by the count of non-null entries. This means a missing salary is excluded from both the numerator and the denominator when you average. If you want nulls to be treated as zeros — for example to reflect that missing commissions are effectively zero percent — you must substitute a value with NVL or COALESCE before aggregating. A concrete example: to compute an average commission treating nulls as zero, replace missing commission with zero and then average. Without substitution, the average would divide by fewer rows and may appear higher. A common misconception is expecting averages to include all employees by default. Always decide whether nulls represent unknowns or zeros for your business question. Try both approaches and compare: which reflects the business intent — excluding unknowns or counting them as zero? SUM and AVG with NULLs and NVL means sum and avg ignore nulls. use nvl or coalesce when a null should be treated as zero or another specific value.. In practical terms, how totals and averages treat missing values and how to include them intentionally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › SUM and AVG with NULLs
Behavior

SUM ignores nulls; AVG ignores nulls in numerator and denominator

Decide whether NULL means unknown or zero. If it should be zero, replace it first with NVL or COALESCE.

• SUM totals only present numeric values; NULLs are not added.
• AVG computes the mean using only non-null entries by default.
• NVL(column, 0) or COALESCE(column, 0) can convert NULL to zero before aggregation.
Example scenario
To compute average commission treating NULL as zero, substitute NULLs first. Otherwise, the average divides by fewer employees and may misrepresent the overall rate.
-- Visual queries (run these in your SQL client)
-- Average commission excluding NULLs
SELECT AVG(commission_pct) FROM employees;

-- Average commission treating NULL as zero
SELECT AVG(NVL(commission_pct, 0)) FROM employees;

-- Total salary (NULLs ignored)
SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees;
Check Your Understanding

Compare the two average results and ask whether NULL represents missing data or a true zero for your business question.

screens.title: MIN and MAX: Finding Extremes
screens.narratorSegment: MIN and MAX identify the smallest and largest values in a set. They work across numeric, text, and date types. For example, MIN on hire date returns the earliest hire date; MAX on salary returns the highest paid employee. Both functions ignore NULL values, so missing entries do not influence the result. A common misunderstanding is expecting MIN or MAX to return a row — they return the value itself. If you also need the row that contains that value, additional querying is required. Another practical note: when MIN and MAX are applied to character data, they follow the database's sort order, which may be alphabetical; for dates and numbers, the semantics are more intuitive. Concrete example: run MIN(hire_date) and MAX(salary) to find earliest hire and top salary. Consider whether NULLs should be considered; if missing values should indicate an unknown extreme, you must handle them explicitly. How would you retrieve the employee who has the highest salary after finding MAX? MIN and MAX: Finding Extremes means they return the smallest or largest value only, ignore nulls, and can be used on numbers, text, or dates.. In practical terms, how to locate smallest and largest values across types and why nulls do not affect them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Concept

Locate smallest and largest values across a set

These functions return the extreme value itself. Use on dates to find earliest hire or on numeric salary to find the maximum pay.

MIN(hire_date)
Returns the earliest hire date. NULLs are ignored.
MAX(salary)
Returns the highest salary. NULLs are ignored.
Use for thresholds and identifying outliers
Works on numbers, text, dates
Does not return the row — only the value
Example outputs
MIN(hire_date): 1997-06-01 (earliest hire) MAX(salary): 24000 (highest salary)
To fetch the full employee row with the top salary, combine the MAX result with a query that selects the row matching that value.
Key Takeaway

MIN and MAX return value extremes and ignore NULLs. If you need the row that holds an extreme, use an additional lookup step.

screens.title: Using DISTINCT inside Aggregates
screens.narratorSegment: DISTINCT inside a group function tells the function to consider only unique values before aggregating. This can be useful when you want to know how many different departments exist or how many distinct job IDs appear. For example, counting distinct department identifiers returns the number of unique departments represented in the employees table, not the total department entries. However, applying DISTINCT to SUM or AVG changes the calculation in ways that may be misleading if not intended, because you will be summing or averaging only unique values rather than every occurrence. A concrete scenario: COUNT distinct department_id tells HR how many unique departments have employees. But SUM distinct salary would total each unique salary only once, which is rarely useful for total payroll. A common pitfall is using DISTINCT by default; instead, ask whether the analysis needs unique values or all instances. Practice with COUNT DISTINCT on job IDs to confirm the behavior. Which report should use distinct values and which should not? Using DISTINCT inside Aggregates means distinct makes aggregates consider unique values only. use it for counting unique categories, not usually for totals.. In practical terms, when distinct changes the result and why to use it carefully. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › DISTINCT inside Aggregates
Definition & Guidance

Consider uniqueness before aggregating

DISTINCT filters duplicate values before the aggregate runs. Use it when you need a unique count or average of distinct values, not when you want totals across all rows.

COUNT DISTINCT
Counts unique categories, e.g., unique department IDs.
AVG DISTINCT
Averages only unique values — often not desired for salary averages.
SUM DISTINCT
Sums each distinct value once — rarely the payroll total you want.
Example
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT department_id) FROM employees returns the number of unique departments with employees.
Key Takeaway

Use DISTINCT when uniqueness is required. Avoid it for totals unless you specifically need to remove duplicate values first.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often make predictable mistakes when using group functions. One frequent error is assuming COUNT(column) counts all rows; remember it counts only non-null values. Another mistake is applying DISTINCT to SUM or AVG without understanding the effect — DISTINCT will remove duplicate values before aggregation, which can dramatically change totals or averages. A third common trap is ignoring NULLs when interpreting averages or sums; nulls are excluded by default and can make averages appear higher than expected if many values are missing. A final pitfall is expecting an aggregate to return details about rows; aggregates return only a summary value and need additional queries to retrieve the corresponding rows. To avoid these mistakes, always ask: which rows were included, were any nulls substituted, and did DISTINCT change the domain? When in doubt, run the non-distinct and distinct forms and compare results. Practice this comparison habit and your aggregated reports will be reliable. Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Common Mistakes and Misconceptions

Frequent pitfalls

Mistake: COUNT(column) ≠ total rows
If the column has NULLs you will undercount. Use COUNT star for total rows.
Mistake: Using DISTINCT indiscriminately
DISTINCT removes duplicates before aggregation and can distort totals or averages.
Mistake: Ignoring NULL semantics
NULLs are excluded from SUM and AVG. Decide if they represent unknowns or zeros and substitute if needed.
Mistake: Expecting aggregates to return rows
Aggregates return values. To get rows that match an extreme value, run a lookup using the aggregate result.
Quick checklist
  • Did you mean total rows or non-null values?
  • Should NULL be treated as zero for your metric?
  • Does DISTINCT match your analytic intent?

screens.title: Interpreting Aggregate Results
screens.narratorSegment: Running an aggregate returns a single value, but your job as an analyst is to interpret what that single value represents. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will learn how S Q L turns many rows into single summary answers using group functions. These functions operate on sets of rows and return one value — a count, total, average, minimum, or maximum — which is essential when you need high-level metrics from tables such as employees. We'll look at how COUNT behaves differently when you count all rows versus only non‑null values, how SUM and AVG ignore nulls unless you convert them, and how MIN and MAX find extremes across text, numbers, or dates. You will also see when to use DISTINCT inside an aggregate and why that choice can change results unexpectedly. Each idea will include a concrete example using a simple employees table, a common misconception to watch for, and a short practice task so you can try the queries yourself. By the end, you'll be able to write queries that summarize payroll, headcount, and ranges with confidence and avoid common mistakes around nulls. Ready to turn row-level data into meaningful summaries?

These objectives focus your practice and assessment. First, you will accurately identify and differentiate the common group functions: count, sum, average, minimum, and maximum. That means you can name what each returns and why it matters in a report. Second, you'll understand that these functions operate over sets of rows to produce a single summary value; you'll be able to explain why a query with no grouping returns one aggregated result. Third, you will apply the DISTINCT keyword inside group functions to count or aggregate only unique values, and know when that gives a different answer from a regular aggregate. Fourth, you will explain how NULL values are handled by different group functions and use NVL or COALESCE when you must treat NULL as a specific value. Each objective includes a brief practice prompt so you can write the actual S Q L and verify results. These skills let you summarize payroll, headcount, and ranges reliably for business reports. We will check your understanding with hands‑on queries and a short assessment. First, you will write queries that return the total number of employees and verify COUNT star. Then you will write SUM and AVG queries to calculate payroll totals and average salary, observing how NULL salaries affect results. You will practice COUNT with a specific column to see how non‑null counting differs from counting all rows. Next, you will compute MIN and MAX for dates and amounts to locate extremes. You will use COUNT DISTINCT to count unique job identifiers and try AVG with NVL to treat null commissions as zero. Each task maps back to a learning objective so you can confirm competence. During assessment, be prepared to explain why a result changed when DISTINCT or NVL was added. This process ensures you not only run queries but also interpret and justify their outputs. Group functions, also called aggregate functions, compute a single summary value from a set of rows. They do not return one result per row; instead they examine a selection of rows and produce one number or value that describes that set. For example, if you ask for the total salary across all employees, you are taking many salary values and producing one total. A concrete example: an employees table with multiple salary entries will yield one SUM value when you sum the salary column. This is different from non-aggregate queries that list each employee. A common misconception is to expect aggregates to preserve row-level detail — they do not. If you need both summaries and details, you must combine aggregates with grouping clauses, but that is outside this screen's core definition. Why it matters: aggregates let you replace tedious manual calculations with a single S Q L expression, which scales to millions of rows. Example scenario: HR wants total payroll for a quarter; a SUM on salary returns that single payroll number instantly. Consider: when you see one aggregated number, ask which rows were included and whether NULL values or DISTINCT uniqueness affected the result. How will you check which rows an aggregate summarized?

COUNT is frequently misused because people assume every COUNT returns the same thing. There are two common forms to know: counting all rows and counting non‑null values in a column. COUNT star counts every row in the chosen set, including rows that have nulls in other columns. By contrast, COUNT with a column name counts only rows where that column is not null. A concrete example: an employees table with five rows, one salary set to null. COUNT star returns five, while counting salary returns four. That difference matters when you report headcount versus the number of employees with salary recorded. A typical misconception is thinking COUNT column equals total rows; this leads to underreporting when nulls exist. When you need the total rows regardless of nulls, use the all-rows form. When you need how many valid entries a column contains, use the column form. Practice: run both forms and compare results to confirm which rows were ignored. SUM and AVG are straightforward in intent but subtle in behavior when nulls are present. SUM totals all non-null numeric values. AVG computes the arithmetic mean of non-null values only, dividing by the count of non-null entries. This means a missing salary is excluded from both the numerator and the denominator when you average. If you want nulls to be treated as zeros — for example to reflect that missing commissions are effectively zero percent — you must substitute a value with NVL or COALESCE before aggregating. Here are the core ideas to keep in mind. Group functions aggregate sets of rows into single summary values: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX. COUNT star counts every row; COUNT of a column counts only non-null entries. SUM and AVG ignore nulls unless you substitute them with NVL or COALESCE. MIN and MAX find extremes across numbers, text, or dates and also ignore nulls. DISTINCT inside an aggregate tells the function to consider only unique values before computing the result, which is helpful for counting categories but usually not for totals. Keep three compact rules in mind. Rule one: COUNT star counts rows; COUNT of a column counts only non-null values. Rule two: SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX ignore NULLs in the aggregated column; use NVL or COALESCE when you must treat missing values as zero or another value. Rule three: DISTINCT inside an aggregate restricts the operation to unique values and can change totals and averages dramatically, so apply it deliberately. These three rules cover most surprises you'll see when summarizing data.
